plain_english:
"Philosophers don't practice everything they preach."

That's true. But they still do a lot of good through their teaching and the noble ideas they develop. I wish they could live up to all their words — imagine how happy they would be! But you have no right to dismiss good advice and hearts full of good intentions. People deserve credit for taking on worthwhile studies, even if they don't see them through to the end.

Why should we be surprised when people who start climbing a steep mountain don't make it to the top? Still, if you're human, show respect for those who attempt great things, even when they fail. It takes a generous spirit to aim not just for what you can handle, but for what humanity itself might achieve. It means having lofty goals and making plans so big that even people with brilliant minds couldn't fully carry them out — people who set these rules for themselves:
original_excerpt: "Philosophers do not carry into effect all that they teach." No; but they effect much good by their teaching, by the noble thoughts which they conceive in their minds: would, indeed, that they could act up to their talk: what could be happier than they would be? but in the meanwhile you have no right to despise good sayings and hearts full of good thoughts. Men deserve praise for engaging in profitable studies, even though they stop short of producing any results. Why need we wonder if those who begin to climb a steep path do not succeed in ascending it very high? yet, if you be a man, look with respect on those who attempt great things, even though they fall. It is the act of a generous spirit to proportion its efforts not to its own strength but to that of human nature, to entertain lofty aims, and to conceive plans which are too vast to be carried into execution even by those who are endowed with gigantic intellects, who appoint for themselves the following rules:

plain_english: I will face death or a comedy with the same calm expression. I will take on any work, no matter how hard, using my mind to strengthen my body. I will despise riches whether I have them or not. If my wealth is gone, I won't be gloomy. If it surrounds me, I won't be more excited than I should be. Whether Fortune comes or goes, I won't even notice her. I will see all lands as if they belong to me, and my own land as if it belongs to everyone. I will live remembering that I was born to serve others, and I will thank Nature for this. How could she have done better for me? She has given me alone to everyone, and everyone to me alone.
original_excerpt: I will look upon death or upon a comedy with the same expression of countenance: I will submit to labours, however great they may be, supporting the strength of my body by that of my mind: I will despise riches when I have them as much as when I have them not; if they be elsewhere I will not be more gloomy, if they sparkle around me I will not be more lively than I should otherwise be: whether Fortune comes or goes I will take no notice of her: I will view all lands as though they belong to me, and my own as though they belonged to all mankind: I will so live as to remember that I was born for others, and will thank Nature on this account: for in what fashion could she have done better for me? she has given me alone to all, and all to me alone.

plain_english: Whatever I own, I won't hoard it like a miser or waste it carelessly. I'll believe that my truest possessions are the ones I've given to people who deserve them. I won't measure my generosity by how much I give or how often — only by how much it means to the person receiving it. No gift is too big if it goes to someone worthy. I won't do things to impress others, but because my conscience tells me it's right. Even when I'm alone, I'll act as if all of Rome is watching me. When I eat and drink, I'll satisfy nature's needs — not stuff myself like a glutton. I'll be kind to my friends and gentle even to my enemies. I'll forgive people before they ask for it, and I'll meet good people halfway. I'll remember that the whole world is my hometown, that the gods are its rulers, and that they're always above and around me, watching everything I do and say.
original_excerpt: Whatever I may possess, I will neither hoard it greedily nor squander it recklessly. I will think that I have no possessions so real as those which I have given away to deserving people: I will not reckon benefits by their magnitude or number, or by anything except the value set upon them by the receiver: I never will consider a gift to be a large one if it be bestowed upon a worthy object. I will do nothing because of public opinion, but everything because of conscience: whenever I do anything alone by myself I will believe that the eyes of the Roman people are upon me while I do it. In eating and drinking my object shall be to quench the desires of Nature, not to fill and empty my belly. I will be agreeable with my friends, gentle and mild to my foes: I will grant pardon before I am asked for it, and will meet the wishes of honourable men half way: I will bear in mind that the world is my native city, that its governors are the gods, and that they stand above and around me, criticizing whatever I do or say.

plain_english: When nature demands my last breath, or when reason tells me it's time to go, I will leave this life. And I will call everyone to witness that I loved having a clear conscience and pursuing good things. I will say that no one's freedom — especially not my own — was hurt because of me. The person who lives by these rules will soar high and try to reach the gods. Even if he fails, he still 'fails in a high emprise.'
original_excerpt:
Whenever either Nature demands my breath again, or reason bids me dismiss it, I will quit this life, calling all to witness that I have loved a good conscience, and good pursuits; that no one's freedom, my own least of all, has been impaired through me." He who sets up these as the rules of his life will soar aloft and strive to make his way to the gods: of a truth, even though he fails, yet he

"Fails in a high emprise."[4]

plain_english: But you, who hate virtue and anyone who tries to be good, are acting exactly as we'd expect. Sick eyes can't stand sunlight. Night creatures run from daylight and scramble back to their holes when dawn breaks. Animals that fear light hide in dark cracks. So go ahead and croak your complaints. Exercise those miserable tongues by attacking good people. Open your jaws wide and bite as hard as you can — you'll break plenty of teeth before you leave so much as a scratch.
original_excerpt: But you, who hate both virtue and those who practise it, do nothing at which we need be surprised, for sickly lights cannot bear the sun, nocturnal creatures avoid the brightness of day, and at its first dawning become bewildered and all betake themselves to their dens together: creatures that fear the light hide themselves in crevices. So croak away, and exercise your miserable tongues in reproaching good men: open wide your jaws, bite hard: you will break many teeth before you make any impression.
